units.name: Period 1: 1491-1607

concepts.intro: Diverse Native societies developed distinct economies and social structures shaped by regional environments.
b: Southwest (Pueblo, Hohokam): irrigated agriculture (maize, beans, squash), adobe/cliff-dwelling architecture, permanent villages
Great Plains: nomadic/semi-nomadic, hunted bison on foot before horses arrived, seasonal migration
Pacific Northwest: abundant salmon fishing supported large, complex, sedentary societies with social hierarchy (potlatch)
Mississippian culture (Cahokia): large agricultural surplus, mound-building, extensive trade networks, complex chiefdoms
Northeast (Iroquois Confederacy): matrilineal clans, longhouses, Great League of Peace united five (later six) nations

concepts.intro: 'God, Gold, and Glory' drove Spanish, Portuguese, French, and English exploration in the 15th-16th centuries.
b: Economic: search for new trade routes to Asia after Ottoman control of land routes raised prices
Religious: Catholic missionary zeal (Spain/France) to convert Native peoples; later Protestant motives for English colonization
Political/glory: national competition for empire and prestige among European monarchies
Technology: caravel ships, astrolabe, and compass made transoceanic voyages feasible
Portugal pioneered African coastal exploration; Spain funded Columbus's westward voyage (1492)

concepts.intro: The transfer of plants, animals, people, diseases, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492 remade both worlds.
b: To the Americas: horses, pigs, cattle, wheat, sugarcane, and devastating diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza)
To Europe/Old World: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco, cacao — potatoes and maize fueled European population growth
Demographic catastrophe: Native populations declined by an estimated 90% in some regions due to disease with no acquired immunity
Labor shortage from Native depopulation was a key cause of the trans-Atlantic African slave trade
Triggered a lasting shift in global diets, economies, and ecosystems (the 'Great Dying' and agricultural revolution)

concepts.intro: Spain built an extractive empire in the Americas based on conquest, labor exploitation, and religious conversion.
b: Conquistadors (Cortes over the Aztec, Pizarro over the Inca) used superior weaponry, disease, and Native rivalries to topple empires
Encomienda system: Crown granted colonists the right to Native labor in exchange for 'protection' and Christianization — functioned as forced labor
Casta system: rigid racial hierarchy (peninsulares, creoles, mestizos, Native peoples, enslaved Africans) structured colonial society
Missions (especially in Florida and the Southwest) aimed to convert and control Native populations
Spain extracted vast silver wealth (Potosi) that fueled European inflation (the 'Price Revolution')

concepts.l: Regional diversity of Native North America
concepts.intro: Before contact, Indigenous peoples adapted to distinct environments, producing very different economies and social structures.
b: Southwest (Pueblo): irrigation-based maize agriculture, adobe towns, sedentary life.
Great Plains: mobile bison hunting on foot (before horses), small bands.
Northeast/Iroquois: mixed farming (the 'three sisters') plus hunting; matrilineal kinship and confederation.
Pacific Northwest: rich salmon fisheries supported large, hierarchical, permanent villages.
Mississippi River Valley (Cahokia): maize surplus fed a large, stratified, mound-building society.

concepts.l: Systems of labor and coerced conversion
concepts.intro: Spain built its American empire on extracting Native labor and imposing Catholicism.
b: The encomienda granted colonists the labor and tribute of Native communities in exchange for 'protection' and Christianization.
The mission system concentrated Native peoples for conversion and labor, often by force.
Bartolome de las Casas condemned the abuses; debate over Native humanity shaped Spanish policy.
A rigid casta system ranked people by ancestry (peninsulares, creoles, mestizos, Native peoples, Africans).
Native resistance persisted, most dramatically in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.

traps: Native American societies were NOT uniform — economy and social structure varied hugely by region/environment.
Disease, not superior weaponry alone, caused most Native depopulation after contact.
The encomienda system was a form of forced labor, not free wage labor, despite the 'protection' rhetoric.
Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, not the mainland North American colonies that came later.
fms: Columbian Exchange = 1492 onward, Old World ↔ New World transfer
Native population decline: disease (~90%) >> warfare as a cause
Disease, not warfare, caused the great majority of Native population decline after 1492.
Encomienda = coerced Native labor + forced Christianization under Spanish rule.

units.name: Period 2: 1607-1754

concepts.intro: Founded for profit, the Chesapeake economy became dependent on tobacco and enslaved labor.
b: Jamestown (1607): first permanent English colony; near-failure from disease and starvation until tobacco cultivation (John Rolfe) made it profitable
Headright system: 50 acres granted per person whose passage was paid, encouraging indentured servitude and population growth
Shift from indentured servants to enslaved Africans accelerated after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) exposed risks of a free ex-servant class
House of Burgesses (1619): first representative assembly in English America
Tobacco monoculture led to large plantations, dispersed settlement, and a rigid social hierarchy with planter elites at the top

concepts.intro: Settled largely by Puritans seeking religious purity, New England developed a distinct economy and tightly-knit town-based society.
b: Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630): Puritans sought to build a 'city upon a hill' (John Winthrop) — a model godly society, not full religious tolerance
Congregationalist church governance influenced town meeting democracy and relatively broad (male) political participation
Economy based on subsistence farming, fishing, shipbuilding, and trade (rocky soil unsuited to cash crops)
Roger Williams (banished) founded Rhode Island on principles of religious toleration and separation of church and state
Salem Witch Trials (1692) reflected social tensions, religious anxiety, and the dangers of mass hysteria

concepts.intro: The Middle colonies were marked by ethnic and religious diversity; the Southern colonies (beyond Chesapeake) built plantation slave societies.
b: Middle colonies (NY, PA, NJ, DE): diverse population (Dutch, Germans, Quakers, English), fertile land ('breadbasket'), religious tolerance especially in Pennsylvania (William Penn, Quakers)
Southern colonies (Carolinas, Georgia): rice and indigo cultivation in South Carolina relied heavily on enslaved labor and Africans' rice-growing expertise
Georgia founded (1733) as a buffer against Spanish Florida and briefly as a haven for debtors before adopting slavery
Growing reliance on slave labor across the South created stark regional economic and social divergence from the North

concepts.intro: The trans-Atlantic slave trade forcibly transported millions of Africans to the Americas, and slavery hardened into a racialized, hereditary institution.
b: Middle Passage: brutal ocean crossing with high mortality rates for enslaved Africans
Triangular trade: manufactured goods (Europe) → enslaved Africans (Africa) → raw materials/cash crops (Americas) → back to Europe
Colonial slave codes (Virginia, 1660s-1705) codified slavery as lifelong, hereditary, and race-based
Stono Rebellion (1739, South Carolina): largest slave uprising in the colonies, led to harsher slave codes
By the mid-1700s, enslaved Africans formed the majority of the population in parts of the Lower South

concepts.intro: England regulated colonial trade to benefit the mother country under the economic theory of mercantilism.
b: Mercantilism: colonies exist to enrich the mother country by supplying raw materials and buying finished goods
Navigation Acts (1651 onward): required colonial goods to be shipped on English ships and certain goods routed through England
'Salutary neglect': before 1754, Britain loosely enforced trade regulations, allowing colonial self-governance and smuggling to flourish
Triangular trade routes linked New England rum, African slaves, and West Indian sugar/molasses

concepts.l: Enlightenment and the First Great Awakening
concepts.intro: Two transatlantic intellectual currents reshaped colonial thought in the early 1700s.
b: The Enlightenment stressed reason, natural rights, and the social contract (Locke), influencing colonial elites.
The First Great Awakening (1730s-40s) was an emotional religious revival led by Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield.
Itinerant preaching and 'New Light' congregations undercut established church authority.
The Awakening was one of the first shared experiences across colonial lines.
Both movements encouraged questioning of traditional authority, a seedbed for revolutionary ideas.

traps: New England was founded for religious purposes; the Chesapeake was founded primarily for profit (tobacco).
Bacon's Rebellion (1676) accelerated the shift from indentured servitude to racial slavery — it did not cause slavery to begin.
Pennsylvania's religious tolerance under Penn was unusually broad for its time, not the colonial norm.
Salutary neglect describes lax enforcement BEFORE 1754 — not a permanent British policy.
fms: Headright = 50 acres per paid passage (Chesapeake)
Navigation Acts = mercantilist trade regulation, enforced loosely until 1754
Mercantilism: colonies exist to enrich the mother country (raw materials out, finished goods in).
The Great Awakening created a common colonial experience and weakened deference to authority.

units.name: Period 3: 1754-1800

concepts.intro: Part of the global Seven Years' War, this conflict between Britain/colonists and France/Native allies reshaped North America and colonial-British relations.
b: Albany Congress (1754): Benjamin Franklin proposed the Albany Plan of Union for colonial cooperation — rejected by colonies but an early step toward unity
Treaty of Paris (1763): France ceded Canada and land east of the Mississippi to Britain; Spain gained Louisiana
Britain's war debt led to new taxation of colonies, ending the era of salutary neglect
Proclamation of 1763: forbade colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains, angering land-hungry colonists
Pontiac's Rebellion: Native uprising against British expansion into the Ohio Valley after the war

concepts.l: Road to Revolution: taxation and resistance
concepts.intro: A series of British revenue acts and colonial resistance escalated tensions from 1764 to 1776.
b: Stamp Act (1765): direct tax on printed materials; sparked 'no taxation without representation' and the Stamp Act Congress
Townshend Acts (1767) taxed imported goods; colonists responded with boycotts and non-importation agreements
Boston Massacre (1770): British soldiers killed five colonists; used as propaganda (Paul Revere's engraving) to inflame anti-British sentiment
Boston Tea Party (1773): Sons of Liberty dumped tea to protest the Tea Act's monopoly for the East India Company
Intolerable/Coercive Acts (1774): punished Massachusetts after the Tea Party, closing Boston Harbor and revoking self-government — prompted the First Continental Congress

concepts.intro: Enlightenment political philosophy and colonial experience with self-government provided the intellectual foundation for independence.
b: John Locke's natural rights (life, liberty, property) and social contract theory heavily influenced the Declaration of Independence
Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) used plain language to make the case for independence and against monarchy
Declaration of Independence (1776, Jefferson): asserted natural rights, listed grievances against George III, declared separation
Republicanism: emphasis on civic virtue, the common good, and rejection of hereditary aristocracy
Salutary neglect had allowed colonial legislatures real power, so many colonists saw new British taxes as violating established rights

concepts.intro: America's first national government (1781-1789) was deliberately weak, reflecting fear of centralized power after British rule.
b: No power to tax, no executive branch, no national judiciary, and each state had one vote regardless of size
Amendments required unanimous consent — made reform nearly impossible
Successes: Northwest Ordinance (1787) established an orderly process for territories to become states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory
Shays' Rebellion (1786-87): armed uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers exposed the Confederation's inability to maintain order or raise an army
Weaknesses (no power to regulate interstate commerce, no unified currency) directly led to calls for a new constitution

concepts.intro: The Constitutional Convention of 1787 created a stronger federal government through compromise, sparking fierce debate over ratification.
b: Great (Connecticut) Compromise: bicameral legislature — House by population, Senate with equal representation (2 per state)
Three-Fifths Compromise: counted enslaved people as 3/5 of a person for representation and taxation purposes
Federalists (Hamilton, Madison, Jay — The Federalist Papers) supported ratification and a strong central government
Anti-Federalists opposed ratification, fearing tyranny and the lack of a bill of rights protecting individual liberties
Bill of Rights (1791): first ten amendments added to secure ratification and protect individual liberties from federal overreach

concepts.l: Washington's presidency and early partisan divide
concepts.intro: The first administration set precedents and saw the emergence of America's first political parties over economic and foreign policy disputes.
b: Hamilton's financial plan: national bank, federal assumption of state debts, tariffs to protect industry — favored a strong central government
Jefferson and Madison opposed Hamilton's loose constitutional interpretation, favoring states' rights and an agrarian republic (strict construction)
Whiskey Rebellion (1794): Washington used federal troops to suppress a tax revolt, demonstrating federal authority
Federalists (Hamilton) vs. Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson) emerged as the first party system
Washington's Farewell Address warned against permanent foreign alliances and domestic political factions

traps: The Three-Fifths Compromise was about representation/taxation, not about the moral status of slavery itself.
The Articles of Confederation failed due to WEAKNESS (no taxing/military power), not because it was too strong.
Anti-Federalists opposed ratification of the Constitution — they did not oppose independence from Britain.
Hamilton favored loose construction and a strong federal government; Jefferson favored strict construction and states' rights — it's easy to mix these up.
fms: Great Compromise = bicameral legislature (House=population, Senate=equal)
3/5 Compromise = enslaved persons counted as 3/5 for representation & taxes
'No taxation without representation': colonists accepted external trade duties but not internal revenue taxes imposed by a Parliament they did not elect.
The Articles of Confederation failed mainly because Congress could not tax or regulate commerce.

units.name: Period 4: 1800-1848

concepts.intro: Andrew Jackson's presidency (1829-1837) expanded suffrage for white men and reshaped the presidency, while deepening exclusion of Native Americans and enslaved people.
b: Expansion of white male suffrage (removal of property requirements) marked the rise of the 'common man' in politics
Spoils system: rewarding political supporters with government jobs, justified as democratizing government
Indian Removal Act (1830) and the Trail of Tears (1838): forced relocation of the Cherokee and other tribes despite Worcester v. Georgia ruling in the Cherokee's favor
Bank War: Jackson vetoed the re-charter of the Second Bank of the U.S., viewing it as an elite monopoly harming ordinary Americans
Nullification Crisis (1832-33): South Carolina claimed the right to nullify the federal tariff; Jackson threatened force, crisis resolved by compromise tariff

concepts.intro: A transportation and communication revolution linked regional economies into a national market, transforming labor and daily life.
b: Erie Canal (1825) connected the Great Lakes to the Hudson River, boosting trade and western settlement
Railroads and steamboats dramatically cut transportation time and costs, expanding markets
Lowell System: young women worked in textile mills under close supervision — early industrial wage labor
Rise of a distinct middle class and the 'cult of domesticity' idealizing women's role in the home as industrial work moved outside it
Regional economic specialization deepened: Northeast industry, Midwest grain, South cotton — increasing sectional interdependence and tension

concepts.intro: A wave of religious revivalism emphasized personal salvation and human perfectibility, fueling a broad array of antebellum reform movements.
b: Revivalism (Charles Finney) stressed individual conversion and the ability to achieve salvation through good works
Temperance movement sought to reduce/ban alcohol consumption, tied to concerns about family and social order
Abolitionism: William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator (1831) and Frederick Douglass demanded immediate emancipation
Seneca Falls Convention (1848): Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments launched the organized women's rights movement
Education reform (Horace Mann) promoted common (public) schools; utopian communities (Oneida, Brook Farm) experimented with alternative social structures

concepts.intro: Americans increasingly believed it was their destiny to expand across the continent, driving territorial acquisition and conflict.
b: Manifest Destiny: belief that American expansion across North America was inevitable and divinely ordained (term coined 1845)
Louisiana Purchase (1803, Jefferson) doubled U.S. territory, despite Jefferson's strict-constructionist doubts about its constitutionality
Texas annexation (1845) and the Mexican-American War (1846-48) resulted in the Mexican Cession (California, New Mexico territory)
Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed banning slavery in territory won from Mexico — failed to pass but intensified sectional conflict
Oregon Trail and Mormon migration to Utah reflected large-scale westward migration in this period

concepts.l: Antebellum politics: the Second Party System
concepts.intro: By the 1830s a stable two-party rivalry organized national politics around economic questions.
b: Democrats (Jackson): limited federal government, hard money, opposition to the national bank, expansion.
Whigs (Clay, Webster): the 'American System' of a national bank, protective tariffs, and internal improvements.
The Nullification Crisis (1832-33): South Carolina claimed a right to void the 'Tariff of Abominations'; Jackson threatened force, and a compromise tariff defused it.
The Bank War: Jackson vetoed the Second Bank's recharter and moved deposits to 'pet banks'.
The Panic of 1837 followed, hurting Van Buren's presidency.

concepts.intro: Expansion repeatedly forced Congress to confront slavery's spread.
b: The Missouri Compromise (1820) admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as free, and banned slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes in the Louisiana Territory.
The 'gag rule' (1836-44) tabled antislavery petitions in the House, angering northerners like John Quincy Adams.
Abolitionism grew: William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator, Frederick Douglass, the American Anti-Slavery Society.
Most white northerners were not abolitionists but increasingly opposed slavery's expansion.
Southern defenders shifted from calling slavery a 'necessary evil' to a 'positive good'.

traps: Jacksonian 'democracy' expanded suffrage for white men while intensifying the removal and disenfranchisement of Native Americans.
The Second Great Awakening's religious revivalism directly fueled reform movements like abolition and temperance — the two are linked, not separate.
The Wilmot Proviso never passed Congress, but it foreshadowed the sectional slavery debate of the 1850s.
Manifest Destiny is a mid-1840s term/ideology, not a formal government policy from the Founding era.
fms: Erie Canal completed 1825 — linked Great Lakes to Atlantic via Hudson
Seneca Falls Convention 1848 — start of organized women's rights movement
The Market Revolution: canals, roads, railroads, and the telegraph knit together a national market economy.
Second Great Awakening reform: temperance, abolition, women's rights (Seneca Falls, 1848), asylum and school reform.

units.name: Period 5: 1844-1877

concepts.intro: Territorial expansion after the Mexican-American War forced the question of slavery's expansion, and a series of failed compromises deepened North-South division.
b: Compromise of 1850: California admitted free, popular sovereignty in Utah/New Mexico territories, stronger Fugitive Slave Act, banned slave trade (not slavery) in D.C.
Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854): introduced popular sovereignty in territories north of the Missouri Compromise line, effectively repealing it and causing 'Bleeding Kansas' violence
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857): Supreme Court ruled enslaved people were not citizens and Congress could not ban slavery in territories, inflaming the North
Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe) galvanized Northern anti-slavery sentiment
Lincoln-Douglas debates (1858) and the election of Lincoln (1860) as a purely sectional (Republican, anti-expansion of slavery) candidate triggered Southern secession

concepts.l: Causes and course of the Civil War
concepts.intro: Secession following Lincoln's election led to four years of war fought over slavery's expansion and, ultimately, the Union's survival.
b: Southern states seceded starting with South Carolina (Dec. 1860), citing states' rights to protect slavery; Confederacy formed (Jefferson Davis)
Fort Sumter (April 1861): first shots of the war, after which Lincoln called for troops and four more states seceded
Union advantages: larger population, industrial capacity, railroads; Confederate advantages: fighting defensively on home ground, strong military leadership early on
Emancipation Proclamation (Jan. 1863): freed enslaved people in Confederate-held territory, reframed the war as a fight to end slavery, and allowed Black enlistment in the Union Army
Turning points: Antietam (1862, enabled the Emancipation Proclamation), Gettysburg and Vicksburg (1863, turned the tide toward the Union)

concepts.intro: After the war (1865-1877), the nation grappled with how to reintegrate the South and define citizenship and rights for formerly enslaved people.
b: 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery; 14th Amendment (1868) granted birthright citizenship and equal protection; 15th Amendment (1870) barred denying the vote based on race
Radical Republicans in Congress pushed for stronger protections for freedpeople than Lincoln's or Andrew Johnson's lenient plans, leading to Johnson's impeachment (1868, acquitted)
Freedmen's Bureau provided education, food, and legal aid to formerly enslaved people during Reconstruction
Black political participation surged (Black officeholders, participation in state constitutional conventions) during Radical Reconstruction
Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction: Republican Hayes won a disputed election in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the South, ending federal protection of Black rights

concepts.intro: White Southern resistance and the withdrawal of federal enforcement allowed a system of racial subordination to replace slavery.
b: Black Codes (immediately postwar) and later Jim Crow laws restricted freedpeople's rights and enforced segregation
Ku Klux Klan and other white supremacist violence terrorized Black communities and their political allies
Sharecropping trapped many freedpeople in cycles of debt, replacing slavery with a new form of economic dependency
Northern war-weariness and a economic depression (Panic of 1873) reduced political will to enforce Reconstruction
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) later legalized 'separate but equal,' cementing the legal framework for segregation that outlived Reconstruction

concepts.intro: A decade of legislative and judicial attempts to settle the slavery question instead deepened the crisis.
b: Compromise of 1850: California free; stronger Fugitive Slave Act; popular sovereignty in the Mexican Cession.
The Fugitive Slave Act radicalized northern opinion and inspired Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852).
Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) repealed the Missouri Compromise line, sparking 'Bleeding Kansas' and destroying the Whig Party.
The Republican Party formed (1854) to stop slavery's expansion.
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) held that Black people were not citizens and that Congress could not bar slavery from territories.

concepts.l: The Union and Confederate home fronts
concepts.intro: Total war reshaped government, society, and the economy on both sides.
b: The Emancipation Proclamation (Jan. 1863) freed enslaved people in Confederate-held areas and allowed Black enlistment.
The Union passed the Homestead Act, Pacific Railway Act, Morrill Land-Grant Act, a national banking system, and an income tax.
Both sides used conscription; the 1863 New York City draft riots turned deadly.
Lincoln suspended habeas corpus in parts of the Union.
Women managed farms and businesses and served as nurses; the Confederacy suffered severe inflation and shortages.

traps: The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people only in Confederate-held territory — not in the loyal border states.
Popular sovereignty (Kansas-Nebraska Act) let TERRITORIES vote on slavery — it did not resolve the debate, it caused violence.
Reconstruction ended in 1877 due to a political compromise, not because racial equality had been achieved.
The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments were passed DURING Reconstruction, not immediately in 1865 all at once.
fms: 13th (1865) = abolished slavery; 14th (1868) = citizenship/equal protection; 15th (1870) = voting rights
Compromise of 1877 = Hayes presidency in exchange for troop withdrawal, ending Reconstruction
The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments abolished slavery, guaranteed citizenship and equal protection, and barred race-based denial of the vote.
Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877: federal troops left the South and Redeemer governments imposed Jim Crow.

units.name: Period 6: 1865-1898

concepts.intro: Rapid industrial growth after the Civil War was driven by new technology, resources, and business consolidation, producing enormous wealth and inequality.
b: Bessemer process cut steel production costs, enabling railroads, skyscrapers, and industrial machinery on a massive scale
Andrew Carnegie (steel) used vertical integration (controlling all stages of production) to dominate his industry
John D. Rockefeller (oil) used horizontal integration and trusts (Standard Oil) to eliminate competitors and control an entire market
Social Darwinism (Herbert Spencer, 'survival of the fittest') was used to justify wealth inequality and oppose government regulation
Transcontinental Railroad (completed 1869) integrated national markets and relied heavily on Chinese and Irish immigrant labor

concepts.l: Gilded Age society: immigration and urbanization
concepts.intro: Mark Twain's 'Gilded Age' term captured a period of glittering wealth masking widespread poverty, urban crowding, and political corruption.
b: 'New immigrants' (Southern/Eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, Jews) arrived in large numbers, differing in religion/culture from earlier 'old immigrants,' fueling nativism
Chinese Exclusion Act (1882): first major law restricting immigration based on nationality, driven by anti-Chinese sentiment in the West
Urbanization: rapid city growth led to overcrowded tenements, political machines (Tammany Hall) that traded services for votes amid corruption
Social Gospel movement and settlement houses (Jane Addams's Hull House) sought to address urban poverty through Christian social action
Political machines and bosses (like Boss Tweed) provided real services to immigrants but were rife with graft and corruption

concepts.intro: Workers organized in response to dangerous conditions, low wages, and long hours in the new industrial economy, often facing violent suppression.
b: Knights of Labor: sought to include all workers (skilled/unskilled, women, Black workers) and broad reforms like the 8-hour day
American Federation of Labor (Samuel Gompers): focused narrowly on 'bread and butter' issues (wages, hours) for skilled workers through collective bargaining
Haymarket Affair (1886): a bombing at a Chicago labor rally led to a public backlash against labor unions, linking them to radicalism/anarchism
Homestead Strike (1892) and Pullman Strike (1894): major strikes crushed by private security and federal troops, showing government often sided with business
Labor's overall gains were limited in this period by court injunctions, an unsympathetic judiciary, and employer strategies like blacklisting

concepts.intro: Farmers, squeezed by falling crop prices, high railroad rates, and debt, organized politically to demand economic reform.
b: Grange movement and Farmers' Alliances organized farmers cooperatively before evolving into the Populist (People's) Party
Populist Party platform (1892, Omaha Platform): called for free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, and government regulation of railroads
Free silver debate: Populists/silverites wanted silver-backed currency to inflate the money supply and ease farmers' debt burden; gold-standard advocates wanted stable currency
William Jennings Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech (1896) championed free silver and won him the Democratic (and Populist) nomination, but he lost to McKinley
Populism's decline after 1896 nonetheless left a legacy of reform ideas later adopted during the Progressive Era

concepts.l: The New South and Southern agriculture
concepts.intro: After Reconstruction the South promoted industry but remained poor, rural, and racially stratified.
b: Boosters like Henry Grady promoted textile mills, tobacco, and railroads, but the region stayed largely agricultural.
Sharecropping and tenant farming trapped Black and poor white farmers in debt through the crop-lien system.
Jim Crow laws mandated segregation; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld 'separate but equal'.
Disenfranchisement via poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses stripped Black men of the vote.
Ida B. Wells led anti-lynching journalism and activism.

concepts.intro: National politics featured close elections, high turnout, machine patronage, and few policy differences.
b: Party loyalty ran high but the parties rarely differed on major issues; the tariff and 'the money question' (gold vs. silver) dominated.
Political machines like Tammany Hall traded services for votes and skimmed graft.
The Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883) created merit-based hiring after Garfield's assassination.
The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) and Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) were early, weak federal regulation.
Farmers and reformers denounced government as captured by railroads and trusts.

traps: Vertical integration (Carnegie, controlling supply chain) differs from horizontal integration (Rockefeller, buying out competitors) — don't confuse the two.
The Knights of Labor were broadly inclusive; the AFL organized only skilled workers — a key contrast.
'New immigrants' (Southern/Eastern Europe, after ~1880s) differ from earlier 'old immigrants' (Northern/Western Europe) — nativist reaction targeted the newer group.
Populism was primarily an agrarian (farmer) movement, distinct from the urban, worker-focused labor movement, though both arose from industrial-era grievances.
fms: Vertical integration = control all production stages (Carnegie/steel); Horizontal integration = buy out competitors (Rockefeller/oil)
Omaha Platform (1892) = free silver, income tax, direct election of senators, railroad regulation
Populist (People's Party) demands: free silver, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, government ownership of railroads.
New immigration (1880s+) shifted from northern/western Europe to southern/eastern Europe, fueling nativism.

units.name: Period 7: 1890-1945

concepts.intro: Progressives responded to the problems of industrialization and urbanization with government activism at the local, state, and federal levels.
b: Muckrakers (Upton Sinclair's The Jungle, Ida Tarbell on Standard Oil) exposed corruption and unsafe conditions, spurring reform legislation like the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906)
Political reforms: initiative, referendum, recall, direct primary, and the 17th Amendment (direct election of senators) aimed to increase direct democracy
Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal: trust-busting (regulating rather than eliminating big business), consumer protection, and conservation of natural resources
Woodrow Wilson's New Freedom: lowered tariffs, created the Federal Reserve System (1913) for banking stability, and the Federal Trade Commission to police unfair business practices
19th Amendment (1920) granted women's suffrage, the culmination of decades of activism by suffragists like Susan B. Anthony and Alice Paul

concepts.intro: The U.S. expanded overseas influence in the late 19th/early 20th century, debating its role as an emerging world power.
b: Spanish-American War (1898): U.S. gained the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam; Cuba became a U.S. protectorate under the Platt Amendment
Anti-Imperialist League opposed annexing the Philippines, arguing it contradicted American democratic principles; imperialists argued for markets, strategic bases, and 'civilizing' missions
Theodore Roosevelt's 'Big Stick' diplomacy and the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine asserted U.S. right to intervene in Latin America
Panama Canal (completed 1914): U.S. backed Panamanian independence from Colombia to secure canal rights, boosting naval and trade power
Open Door Policy (China, 1899-1900): sought equal trade access for all nations in China rather than territorial division

concepts.intro: The U.S. entered WWI in 1917 after years of neutrality, and the war's aftermath reshaped domestic society and foreign policy debates.
b: Causes of U.S. entry: unrestricted German submarine warfare (sinking of the Lusitania, 1915) and the Zimmermann Telegram (1917, Germany proposed alliance with Mexico)
Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points proposed self-determination and a League of Nations for lasting peace
Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles and League of Nations membership, reflecting a return to isolationist sentiment
Wartime mobilization: Great Migration of African Americans to Northern industrial cities; expanded roles for women in the workforce
Wartime repression: Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918) restricted anti-war speech, upheld in Schenck v. United States (1919, 'clear and present danger')

concepts.intro: The postwar decade saw cultural conflict between traditionalism and modernity, economic boom, and rising nativism.
b: Economic boom fueled by mass production (assembly line), consumer credit, and new consumer goods (automobiles, radios)
Harlem Renaissance: flourishing of African American art, literature, and music (jazz), centered in New York

Cultural clashes: Scopes Trial (1925, evolution vs. fundamentalism), Prohibition (18th Amendment) and its widespread evasion, and a revived KKK targeting immigrants, Catholics, Jews, and Black Americans
Immigration restriction: National Origins Act (1924) set strict quotas favoring Northern/Western Europe, reflecting nativism
Republican pro-business policies (Harding, Coolidge, Hoover): low taxes, high tariffs (Fordney-McCumber), minimal regulation

concepts.l: The Great Depression and New Deal
concepts.intro: The 1929 stock market crash triggered a decade-long economic collapse, met by Franklin Roosevelt's unprecedented federal response.
b: Causes of the Depression: stock market speculation/margin buying, bank failures, overproduction, uneven income distribution, and the crash of Oct. 1929
Hoover's limited response (voluntary cooperation, Reconstruction Finance Corporation) was seen as inadequate; contrasted with FDR's activist New Deal

New Deal relief/recovery/reform: Social Security Act (1935, retirement pensions), FDIC (bank deposit insurance), TVA (regional development), Wagner Act (protected union organizing/collective bargaining)

Critics from the left (Huey Long) argued the New Deal did too little; critics from the right and the Supreme Court (which struck down NIRA, AAA) argued it did too much and was unconstitutional overreach
The New Deal did not end the Depression (which persisted until WWII mobilization) but permanently expanded the federal government's role in the economy and social welfare

concepts.intro: The U.S. entered WWII after Pearl Harbor, mobilizing fully for a two-front war and emerging as a global superpower.
b: Pearl Harbor attack (Dec. 7, 1941) by Japan brought the U.S. into the war against the Axis powers (Germany, Italy, Japan)
Wartime mobilization: full employment, rationing, war bond drives, and massive industrial conversion to war production ('Arsenal of Democracy')
Japanese American internment (Executive Order 9066): forced relocation of ~120,000 Japanese Americans, later upheld in Korematsu v. United States (1944) and widely condemned in retrospect
Women (Rosie the Riveter) and African Americans entered war-industry jobs in unprecedented numbers, laying groundwork for later civil rights and gender equity movements
Atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (Aug. 1945) ended the war with Japan and opened the nuclear/Cold War era

traps: Progressives sought to REGULATE big business (trust-busting, oversight), not necessarily abolish capitalism.
The U.S. rejected the Treaty of Versailles/League of Nations due to Senate opposition, even though Wilson championed it.
The New Deal did not end the Great Depression — WWII mobilization did, through massive government spending and full employment.
Japanese American internment targeted citizens and immigrants alike based on ancestry, not on any evidence of individual disloyalty.
fms: 19th Amendment (1920) = women's suffrage
Pearl Harbor attack: December 7, 1941 — brought U.S. into WWII
Progressive amendments: 16th (income tax), 17th (direct election of senators), 18th (Prohibition), 19th (woman suffrage).
The New Deal's 'Three Rs': Relief (jobs, aid), Recovery (spending, price supports), Reform (Social Security, SEC, Wagner Act).

units.name: Period 8: 1945-1980

concepts.l: Origins and course of the Cold War
concepts.intro: Ideological conflict between the U.S. (capitalism/democracy) and USSR (communism) defined global politics without direct military conflict between the superpowers.
b: Containment (George Kennan): core U.S. strategy to prevent the spread of communism without direct war with the USSR
Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged support to nations resisting communism; Marshall Plan (1948) provided economic aid to rebuild Western Europe
NATO (1949) formed a Western military alliance; Warsaw Pact (1955) was the Soviet counter-alliance — divided Europe into blocs
Korean War (1950-53): first major 'hot' proxy conflict of containment, ending in stalemate near the original 38th parallel border
Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): closest the U.S. and USSR came to direct nuclear war, resolved through negotiation (Soviet missile removal for a secret U.S. pledge on Turkey missiles)

concepts.intro: African Americans and allies used legal challenges, nonviolent protest, and grassroots organizing to dismantle legal segregation and expand civil rights.
b: Brown v. Board of Education (1954): overturned Plessy's 'separate but equal,' ruling school segregation unconstitutional
Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56, sparked by Rosa Parks) launched Martin Luther King Jr.'s leadership and the nonviolent direct-action strategy
Civil Rights Act (1964): banned discrimination in public accommodations and employment based on race, sex, religion, or national origin
Voting Rights Act (1965): eliminated literacy tests and authorized federal oversight of voter registration in discriminatory jurisdictions
Shift toward Black Power (Malcolm X, Stokely Carmichael) in the late 1960s reflected frustration with the pace of change and emphasized Black self-determination

concepts.intro: President Lyndon Johnson expanded the New Deal's legacy with an ambitious set of programs targeting poverty and inequality.
b: Medicare (health coverage for the elderly) and Medicaid (health coverage for the poor) created lasting federal health programs (1965)
War on Poverty included Head Start (early education), Job Corps, and food stamp expansion
Immigration and Nationality Act (1965) abolished the national-origins quota system, dramatically reshaping U.S. immigration patterns
Environmental and consumer protection laws (EPA created 1970) grew out of 1960s activism (Rachel Carson's Silent Spring)
Great Society programs expanded the federal government's role in social welfare far beyond the New Deal's scope

concepts.l: Vietnam War and its domestic impact
concepts.intro: U.S. involvement in Vietnam, justified by containment logic, escalated into a costly, divisive war that fractured domestic consensus on Cold War policy.
b: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) gave President Johnson broad authority to escalate U.S. military involvement without a formal declaration of war
Tet Offensive (1968): though a military defeat for the Viet Cong/North Vietnam, it shocked American public opinion and undermined confidence in official war reports
Anti-war movement grew on college campuses and among the broader public, including incidents like the Kent State shootings (1970)
Vietnamization (Nixon): gradual withdrawal of U.S. troops while transferring combat duties to South Vietnamese forces
War Powers Act (1973) sought to limit the president's ability to commit troops without congressional approval, a direct legacy of Vietnam

concepts.intro: The era's activism expanded beyond civil rights to feminism, environmentalism, and other identity- and rights-based movements, amid economic difficulty and political scandal.
b: Second-wave feminism (Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, NOW) pushed for workplace equality; Roe v. Wade (1973) established a constitutional right to abortion
Environmental movement gained momentum (first Earth Day, 1970) alongside new federal regulatory agencies
Watergate scandal (1972-74): break-in and cover-up led to Nixon's resignation (1974), deepening public distrust of government
Stagflation (simultaneous inflation and unemployment) in the 1970s challenged existing Keynesian economic policy and hurt Democratic political fortunes
Détente (Nixon): a policy of easing Cold War tensions with the USSR and opening relations with Communist China (1972 visit)

concepts.intro: Sustained prosperity after 1945 transformed where and how Americans lived.
b: The GI Bill funded college and low-cost mortgages for millions of veterans.
Levittown-style mass-produced suburbs, the interstate highway system (1956), and cheap cars drove suburban growth.
Consumer culture, television, and a postwar baby boom reshaped family life.
Population and industry shifted to the Sun Belt (South and West).
Federal mortgage policy and restrictive covenants excluded most Black families from the suburbs, deepening residential segregation.

traps: Containment aimed to STOP the spread of communism, not to roll back or defeat the USSR directly (that was 'rollback,' a more aggressive minority view).
Brown v. Board (1954) addressed school segregation specifically; broader public accommodations discrimination was addressed later by the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
The Tet Offensive was a military defeat for the communist forces but a psychological/political turning point against U.S. public support for the war.
Détente eased tensions with the USSR/China but did NOT end the Cold War — it continued into the 1980s.
fms: Brown v. Board (1954) overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) — two distinct landmark laws
Containment (Kennan) guided US Cold War policy: the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, and Korea.
Key civil rights landmarks: Brown v. Board (1954), the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

units.name: Period 9: 1980-present

concepts.intro: Ronald Reagan's presidency (1981-1989) marked a conservative shift in American politics, emphasizing tax cuts, deregulation, and a renewed Cold War posture.
b: Reaganomics ('supply-side'/trickle-down economics): large tax cuts intended to spur investment and growth, paired with deep domestic spending cuts
Deregulation reduced federal oversight of industries (banking, airlines), continuing a trend begun under Carter
Massive defense spending increases (including the Strategic Defense Initiative, 'Star Wars') pressured the Soviet economy
Federal budget deficits and national debt grew substantially despite the goal of smaller government
Conservative resurgence included the rise of the religious right (Moral Majority) as a political force

concepts.intro: A combination of Soviet economic weakness, reform efforts, and Western pressure led to the collapse of Soviet communism by the early 1990s.
b: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms — glasnost (openness) and perestroika (economic restructuring) — unintentionally accelerated the USSR's collapse
Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) symbolized the end of Soviet control over Eastern Europe
Soviet Union formally dissolved in 1991, ending the Cold War and leaving the U.S. as the world's sole superpower
Persian Gulf War (1991): U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraq from Kuwait, showcasing post-Cold War U.S. military leadership
End of the Cold War prompted debates over America's new global role and the 'peace dividend' of reduced defense spending

concepts.intro: The late 20th/early 21st century saw accelerating economic integration, technological change, and debate over free trade's costs and benefits.
b: NAFTA (1994) created a free trade zone among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, sparking debate over job outsourcing versus lower consumer costs
Rise of the internet and information technology transformed communication, business, and the economy (dot-com boom of the late 1990s)
Deindustrialization: decline of traditional manufacturing jobs, particularly in the 'Rust Belt,' as production shifted overseas
Income inequality widened as wages for many workers stagnated while wealth concentrated among high earners
Financial deregulation and complex mortgage-backed securities contributed to the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession

concepts.intro: Terrorism, prolonged wars, economic crisis, and deep political polarization have defined the 21st century so far.
b: September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks led to the War on Terror, the USA PATRIOT Act (expanded surveillance/law enforcement powers), and creation of the Department of Homeland Security
U.S. invasions of Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003) became the longest wars in U.S. history, with debated justifications and outcomes
2008 financial crisis triggered the Great Recession; federal response included TARP bailouts and later the Affordable Care Act (2010) expanding health coverage
Political polarization intensified, marked by deep partisan divides over immigration, healthcare, race, and the role of government

Ongoing debates over climate change, technology's societal role, racial justice movements (e.g., following George Floyd's murder in 2020), and America's global leadership continue to shape contemporary politics

concepts.intro: From the 1980s on, cultural and religious conflicts increasingly divided the parties.
b: The Religious Right (Moral Majority) mobilized evangelical voters around abortion, school prayer, and family issues.
Debates over affirmative action, gun rights, LGBTQ rights, and immigration hardened partisan lines.
Talk radio, cable news, and later social media reinforced ideological divisions.
The 2000 election was decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore.
Congressional gridlock and party-line voting became the norm.

concepts.l: The 2008 financial crisis and its aftermath
concepts.intro: The worst downturn since the Great Depression reshaped economic policy and politics.
b: A housing bubble built on subprime mortgages and complex securities collapsed in 2007-08.
Major financial firms failed or were rescued; Congress passed the TARP bailout.
Unemployment neared 10%; the Obama administration passed a large stimulus and the Dodd-Frank regulatory law.
The Affordable Care Act (2010) expanded health coverage and became a lasting partisan flashpoint.
The Tea Party and later movements on the left reflected deep distrust of elites and government.

traps: Reaganomics called for smaller government, yet federal deficits and debt actually GREW during his presidency due to tax cuts plus increased defense spending.
The Soviet Union's collapse (1991) resulted from internal economic weakness and Gorbachev's reforms, not from a single U.S. military victory.
NAFTA (1994) is a free-trade agreement among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico — not a global or worldwide trade organization.
The Great Recession began with the 2008 financial crisis, rooted in the housing/mortgage market and financial deregulation, not a stock market bubble alone like 1929.
fms: Berlin Wall fell 1989; USSR dissolved 1991 — end of the Cold War
September 11, 2001 — led to the War on Terror and USA PATRIOT Act
Reaganomics: tax cuts, deregulation, reduced domestic spending, and increased defense spending ('supply-side').
The Cold War ended (1989-91) with the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Early-19th-century transportation/communication boom (canals, railroads) that linked regional economies into one national market.

Corn, beans, and squash grown together by many eastern Native peoples in a mutually supportive planting system.
The idea that colonies exist to enrich the mother country; the Navigation Acts required key colonial trade to pass through England on English ships.
A 1730s-40s religious revival (Edwards, Whitefield) that spread emotional faith, challenged church authority, and created a shared colonial experience.
A Puritan compromise granting partial church membership to the unconverted children of members, responding to declining piety.

Federalist laws restricting immigrants and criminalizing criticism of the government; opposed by the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.
Statements by Madison and Jefferson asserting that states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws (an early nullification argument).
The expansion of white male suffrage and a political culture celebrating the 'common man,' alongside Indian removal and the spoils system.
South Carolina's attempt to void a federal tariff; Jackson threatened force and a compromise tariff resolved it, foreshadowing secession arguments.

The movement of African Americans from the rural South to northern cities for jobs and to escape Jim Crow, beginning around WWI.
Relief (jobs and aid), Recovery (spending and price supports), Reform (Social Security, the SEC, the Wagner Act).

Federal and private practices denying mortgages in Black neighborhoods, excluding Black families from the suburbs and building a wealth gap.

quiz.q: Which best explains the massive decline of the Native American population after 1492?
o: Direct military defeat by European armies in prolonged pitched battles across the continent
Forced mass conversion to Christianity that led Native peoples to abandon traditional farming
Voluntary migration of Native peoples away from European settlements into the far interior
Disease introduced by Europeans, to which Native peoples had no immunity
quiz.e: Diseases like smallpox devastated Native populations who had no acquired immunity, far exceeding deaths from warfare.

quiz.q: The encomienda system in Spanish America primarily provided colonists with:
o: The right to claim free land grants from the crown in exchange for settling and farming it
A form of local representative government in exchange for paying taxes to Spain
The right to Native labor in exchange for 'protecting' and converting them
Direct control over silver shipments in exchange for defending the colony from other empires
quiz.e: Encomienda granted colonists Native labor in exchange for nominal protection and Christianization — functionally forced labor.

quiz.q: Which Native society was known for mound-building and extensive trade networks before European contact?
o: Iroquois
Pueblo
Mississippian (Cahokia)
Plains nomads
quiz.e: The Mississippian culture, centered at sites like Cahokia, built massive mounds and maintained extensive trade networks.

quiz.q: The Columbian Exchange introduced which crop to the Americas from the Old World?
o: Maize
Potatoes
Wheat
Tobacco
quiz.e: Wheat traveled from the Old World to the Americas; maize, potatoes, and tobacco moved the opposite direction.

quiz.q: What was a primary motive for Spanish exploration and colonization?
o: Establishing representative democracy
Religious conversion and extraction of wealth (gold/silver)
Ending the slave trade
Industrial manufacturing
quiz.e: Spain's exploration was driven by 'God, Gold, and Glory' — religious conversion and the pursuit of precious metals.

quiz.q: The labor shortage caused by Native American depopulation was a key cause of:
o: The Atlantic slave trade
The Protestant Reformation
The Columbian Exchange
European unification
quiz.e: As Native labor declined from disease, European colonizers turned to the forced importation of enslaved Africans.

quiz.q: Which technology enabled transoceanic European exploration in this period?
o: The steam engine
The caravel and the astrolabe
The telegraph
The cotton gin
quiz.e: The caravel (ship design) and astrolabe (navigation tool) were key technologies enabling long ocean voyages.

quiz.q: The Iroquois Confederacy was notable for its:
o: Nomadic bison hunting on the Great Plains and seasonal tipi villages
Matrilineal clan structure and the Great League of Peace
Adobe cliff dwellings and irrigated farming in the arid Southwest
A strict Spanish-style hierarchy of nobles, priests, and tribute-paying commoners
quiz.e: The Iroquois Confederacy united nations under matrilineal clans and a council system known as the Great League of Peace.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a typical European motive for exploration?
o: Religious conversion
Economic gain/new trade routes
National glory and prestige
Establishing worker labor unions
quiz.e: Labor unions did not exist in this era; exploration was driven by religion, economics, and national prestige.

quiz.q: Which Native economy relied heavily on salmon fishing to support large, sedentary, socially stratified societies?
o: Great Plains
Pacific Northwest
Southwest Pueblo
Northeast Iroquois
quiz.e: Pacific Northwest societies relied on abundant salmon, supporting complex, permanent settlements with social hierarchy.

quiz.q: The Columbian Exchange is best defined as:
o: A one-way transfer of crops, gold, and silver from the Americas to enrich Europe
A trade agreement dividing the new lands between Spain and Portugal at the Treaty of Tordesillas
A two-way transfer of plants, animals, disease, and people between hemispheres
A religious movement spreading Catholic missions and conversion across the New World
quiz.e: It was a two-way exchange affecting both the Old and New Worlds biologically, demographically, and economically.

quiz.q: What was a major consequence of Spanish silver extraction (e.g., from Potosi)?
o: European inflation (Price Revolution)
The end of the Atlantic slave trade
American independence
Native population growth
quiz.e: The massive influx of Spanish silver caused significant inflation in Europe, known as the Price Revolution.

quiz.q: Which factor most enabled Spanish conquistadors to defeat large Native empires like the Aztec and Inca?
o: Overwhelming numbers of soldiers, as Spanish armies far outnumbered Aztec and Inca forces
Disease, superior weaponry, and exploiting Native rivalries
Peaceful negotiation and voluntary surrender of Native rulers to Spanish authority
Direct military support from other Native nations that remained loyal to Spain throughout
quiz.e: Spanish conquest exploited disease's devastating effects, technological/weapon advantages, and existing rivalries among Native groups.

quiz.q: The casta system in Spanish colonial society was based on:
o: Religious denomination only
A racial hierarchy determining social status
Age and gender only
Region of origin within Spain only
quiz.e: The casta system created a rigid racial hierarchy structuring colonial Spanish American society.

quiz.q: Before European contact, which description best fits Native American societies as a whole?
o: Highly diverse economies and social structures shaped by regional environment
A single unified culture sharing one language, religion, and government across the continent
Entirely nomadic lifeways with no permanent settlements, farming, or trade networks
Universally centered on maritime trade and fishing along the coasts
quiz.e: Native societies varied enormously by region — from Pueblo agriculture to Plains nomadism to Pacific Northwest fishing economies.

quiz.q: The headright system in Virginia was designed to:
o: Abolish indentured servitude and replace it with wage labor on small farms
Grant land only to enslaved Africans who had completed years of service to planters
Encourage immigration and provide labor by granting land per paid passage
Fund the Church of England through land taxes collected from every colonist
quiz.e: Headrights granted 50 acres per person whose passage was paid, encouraging population growth and indentured servitude.

quiz.q: Which colony was founded primarily for religious purposes, seeking to build a model godly society?
o: Virginia
Massachusetts Bay
Georgia
South Carolina
quiz.e: Puritans founded Massachusetts Bay to build a 'city upon a hill' — a model of religious purity, per John Winthrop.

quiz.q: Bacon's Rebellion (1676) is significant because it:
o: Ended slavery in Virginia by forcing planters to free enslaved laborers
Established the House of Burgesses as the colony's first representative assembly
Accelerated the shift from indentured servitude to racial slavery
Caused the Salem Witch Trials by spreading fear throughout the colonies
quiz.e: The rebellion exposed the dangers of a growing class of poor free ex-servants, prompting elites to prefer enslaved labor instead.

quiz.q: The Navigation Acts were a key tool of which economic policy?
o: Free trade
Mercantilism
Socialism
Laissez-faire capitalism
quiz.e: The Navigation Acts enforced mercantilist policy, requiring colonial trade to benefit England.

quiz.q: Which colony was known for religious tolerance under the leadership of William Penn?
o: Massachusetts
Pennsylvania
Virginia
South Carolina
quiz.e: Pennsylvania, founded by Quaker William Penn, was known for unusual religious tolerance for the era.

quiz.q: 'Salutary neglect' refers to Britain's policy of:
o: Strictly enforcing all colonial trade laws before 1754 and restricting colonial autonomy
Imposing direct taxes on the colonies without their consent after 1763
Loosely enforcing trade regulations before 1754, allowing colonial autonomy
Stationing a large military force in the colonies to occupy major port cities
quiz.e: Salutary neglect describes lax British enforcement before 1754, which allowed colonial self-governance and smuggling to flourish.

quiz.q: The Stono Rebellion (1739) resulted in:
o: The abolition of slavery in South Carolina
Harsher slave codes across the South
Immediate emancipation for all enslaved people
The founding of Georgia
quiz.e: After the largest colonial slave uprising, South Carolina and other colonies enacted harsher, more restrictive slave codes.

quiz.q: Which best describes the Middle Colonies?
o: Homogeneous Puritan population governed by church-centered town meetings
Ethnically and religiously diverse, known as the 'breadbasket' colonies
Entirely dependent on tobacco monoculture and a large enslaved labor force
Founded solely as a haven for debtors seeking a fresh start in the New World
quiz.e: The Middle Colonies had diverse populations (Dutch, German, English, Quaker) and fertile farmland earning the 'breadbasket' label.

quiz.q: The Middle Passage refers to:
o: The colonial trade route carrying rum and fish between New England and England
A path used by settlers moving west through the Appalachian mountains
The passage of the Navigation Acts regulating colonial shipping through English ports
The brutal ocean voyage transporting enslaved Africans to the Americas
quiz.e: The Middle Passage was the deadly transatlantic voyage that forcibly transported enslaved Africans.

quiz.q: The House of Burgesses (1619) is significant as:
o: The first Catholic church built in the English colonies by Maryland settlers
The first representative legislative assembly in English America
The first American newspaper printed and distributed in the colonies
The first colonial university, founded to train ministers
quiz.e: Established in Virginia, it was the first elected representative body in the English colonies.

quiz.q: Why did South Carolina rely heavily on enslaved labor for rice cultivation?
o: Rice required no specialized skill, so any laborer could grow it successfully
Enslaved Africans brought rice-growing expertise from West Africa
Rice was grown only by indentured servants who agreed to work in swamps
Rice cultivation was outlawed for free laborers by the colonial legislature
quiz.e: Many enslaved Africans came from rice-growing regions of West Africa and brought valuable agricultural expertise.

quiz.q: Colonial slave codes in Virginia (1660s-1705) established slavery as:
o: Temporary and reversible
Lifelong, hereditary, and race-based
Optional for enslaved individuals
Limited to non-Christians only
quiz.e: These codes codified slavery as a permanent, hereditary, racially defined status.

quiz.q: Which of these was a defining feature of New England town life?
o: Large isolated plantations worked by enslaved laborers growing cash crops
Rice and indigo plantations along the swampy coastal lowlands
Widespread use of the encomienda system to control Native labor
Town meetings and Congregationalist church governance
quiz.e: New England towns centered on Congregationalist churches and relatively democratic town meetings.

quiz.q: The triangular trade linked which three regions?
o: Europe, Africa, and the Americas
Asia, Europe, and Africa
North America, South America, and Asia
England, France, and Spain
quiz.e: Manufactured goods, enslaved Africans, and raw materials/cash crops circulated among Europe, Africa, and the Americas.

quiz.q: Roger Williams founded Rhode Island primarily to promote:
o: Religious toleration and separation of church and state
Strict Puritan orthodoxy and enforcement of Congregationalist church membership
A profitable tobacco economy based on large plantations and indentured servants
A military alliance with Native tribes against English colonial authorities
quiz.e: Williams, banished from Massachusetts Bay, founded Rhode Island on principles of religious freedom and separation of church/state.

quiz.q: By the mid-1700s, the population of the Lower South was increasingly:
o: Majority enslaved African in some areas
Entirely composed of indentured servants
Free of any slave labor
Majority Native American
quiz.e: Enslaved Africans formed the majority population in parts of the Lower South by the mid-18th century due to plantation agriculture.

quiz.q: The Albany Congress (1754) proposed the Albany Plan of Union, which:
o: United the colonies against Britain permanently and created a standing colonial army
Was an early, ultimately rejected step toward colonial cooperation
Ended the French and Indian War by settling land claims with France
Established the Continental Congress as the governing body of the colonies
quiz.e: Franklin's plan for colonial unity was rejected by the colonies but foreshadowed later cooperative efforts.

quiz.q: The Proclamation of 1763 angered colonists because it:
o: Raised taxes on tea imported into the colonies from the East India Company
Ended the fur trade with Native peoples throughout the Ohio Valley
Established the Stamp Act requiring printed materials to carry a tax stamp
Forbade settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
quiz.e: The Proclamation restricted westward expansion, frustrating land-hungry colonists after the costly war.

quiz.q: The phrase 'no taxation without representation' arose in protest of:
o: The Stamp Act
The Emancipation Proclamation
The Missouri Compromise
The Wagner Act
quiz.e: Colonists protested the Stamp Act (1765) as illegitimate direct taxation without their consent via Parliament.

quiz.q: John Locke's philosophy directly influenced the Declaration of Independence through the concept of:
o: Natural rights (life, liberty, property) and government by consent
Divine right of kings and the belief that monarchs rule by God's will
Mercantilism and the belief that colonies exist to enrich the mother country
Social Darwinism and the belief that the fittest individuals should rule
quiz.e: Locke's natural rights and social contract theory underpin Jefferson's arguments in the Declaration.

quiz.q: The main weakness of the Articles of Confederation was:
o: Lack of power to tax or maintain a standing army
Too much centralized power in a national government that overrode the states
An overly powerful executive branch that could veto acts of Congress
A national judiciary that could overrule state laws and courts
quiz.e: The Articles created a deliberately weak national government with no power to tax or field an army, crippling its effectiveness.

quiz.q: Shays' Rebellion (1786-87) demonstrated:
o: The strength of the Articles of Confederation in suppressing internal unrest
Widespread support among farmers for British reoccupation of the states
The Confederation government's inability to maintain order or raise funds
The success of the Bill of Rights in protecting debtors from foreclosure
quiz.e: The armed uprising of indebted farmers showed the Confederation government could not effectively respond to internal unrest.

quiz.q: The Three-Fifths Compromise addressed:
o: The abolition of the slave trade and gradual emancipation in the Northern states
Equal representation for small states in the new national legislature
Representation and taxation counting of enslaved people
Term limits and the method of election for the president
quiz.e: It counted enslaved people as 3/5 of a person for apportioning representatives and direct taxes.

quiz.q: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise created:
o: A unicameral legislature
A bicameral legislature with the House based on population and Senate with equal representation
A single national executive council
Direct popular election of the president
quiz.e: The compromise balanced large and small state interests via a bicameral Congress.

quiz.q: Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the Constitution mainly because:
o: They wanted to restore a monarchy to provide stability after the Revolution
They feared a strong central government would threaten individual liberties without a bill of rights
They supported the Articles of Confederation's taxing power and a national army
They wanted the states to remain part of Britain as self-governing dominions
quiz.e: Anti-Federalists feared federal overreach and demanded a bill of rights to protect individual liberties.

quiz.q: Hamilton's financial plan included all of the following EXCEPT:
o: A national bank
Federal assumption of state debts
Protective tariffs
Abolition of the national debt
quiz.e: Hamilton's plan managed and consolidated debt rather than abolishing it; it included a bank, debt assumption, and tariffs.

quiz.q: The Whiskey Rebellion (1794) is significant because Washington's response demonstrated:
o: Federal weakness in enforcing its laws against armed resistance in frontier regions
Sympathy for tax protesters and a decision to repeal the excise tax on whiskey
The federal government's willingness and ability to enforce its authority
The end of federal taxation of western farmers after the uprising
quiz.e: Washington used federal troops to suppress the tax revolt, asserting federal authority under the new Constitution.

quiz.q: Common Sense by Thomas Paine argued primarily for:
o: Reconciliation with Britain
American independence and against monarchy
Continued colonial loyalty to the king
A return to salutary neglect
quiz.e: Paine's widely read pamphlet made a persuasive, accessible case for independence and republican government.

quiz.q: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) was significant because it:
o: Established a process for territories to become states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory
Created the first national bank and a system for paying the national debt
Ended the French and Indian War and set the boundaries for western settlement
Established the electoral college and a process for choosing presidents
quiz.e: It provided an orderly path to statehood and prohibited slavery in the territory, one of the Confederation's few successes.

quiz.q: The first American political party system emerged over disagreements between:
o: Whigs and Democrats over the Second Bank of the United States and Jackson's policies
Hamilton's Federalists and Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans
Republicans and Populists over free silver and railroad regulation
Progressives and Conservatives over trust-busting and labor reform
quiz.e: Hamilton (strong federal government, loose construction) and Jefferson (states' rights, strict construction) led opposing early parties.

quiz.q: The Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution primarily to:
o: Secure ratification by protecting individual liberties from federal overreach
Increase federal taxing power to pay off the debts left by the Revolution
Abolish slavery and extend civil rights to all free Black Americans
Establish a national bank and a uniform currency for the states
quiz.e: Anti-Federalist concerns about a lack of explicit rights protections led to the Bill of Rights as a condition for broader support.

quiz.q: Jacksonian Democracy expanded political participation primarily for:
o: All adult citizens regardless of race or sex, including women and free Black men
Native Americans, who gained citizenship and voting rights under Jackson
Enslaved people, who gained expanded legal protections under Jackson
White men, through the removal of property requirements for voting
quiz.e: Suffrage expansion under Jackson applied to white men; Native Americans and enslaved people faced increased exclusion/oppression.

quiz.q: The Indian Removal Act (1830) led directly to:
o: The Missouri Compromise
The Trail of Tears
The Nullification Crisis
The Bank War
quiz.e: The Act authorized forced relocation of tribes like the Cherokee, resulting in the deadly Trail of Tears.

quiz.q: The Erie Canal's completion (1825) primarily contributed to:
o: The end of slavery in the Southern states by cutting off cotton exports
The start of the Civil War by dividing Northern and Southern trade
Linking the Great Lakes region to Atlantic trade, boosting the Market Revolution
The Louisiana Purchase by opening the Mississippi River to American shipping
quiz.e: The canal connected western agricultural regions to Eastern markets, a key part of the Market Revolution.

quiz.q: The Second Great Awakening most directly fueled which reform movement?
o: Abolitionism
Mercantilism
Nullification
Manifest Destiny
quiz.e: Religious revivalism's emphasis on human perfectibility and moral action fueled abolitionist and other reform movements.

quiz.q: The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) is best known for:
o: Launching the organized women's rights movement with the Declaration of Sentiments
Ending slavery in the Northern states through a new abolition law
Establishing the Second Bank of the United States as a national currency regulator
Beginning the Mexican-American War by declaring American claims in Texas
quiz.e: The convention, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, produced the Declaration of Sentiments demanding women's rights.

quiz.q: The Wilmot Proviso (1846) proposed to:
o: Ban slavery in territory won from Mexico
Expand slavery into all new territories
Abolish slavery nationwide
End the Mexican-American War
quiz.e: Though it never passed, the Proviso's proposal to ban slavery in Mexican Cession territory intensified sectional tensions.

quiz.q: The Lowell System employed primarily:
o: Enslaved laborers
Young unmarried women in textile mills
Native American workers
Formerly indentured servants
quiz.e: The Lowell mills in Massachusetts employed young women under close supervision, an early industrial wage-labor model.

quiz.q: Jackson's veto of the Second Bank of the United States reflected his view that the bank:
o: Was an elite monopoly harming ordinary Americans
Was too weak to control inflation
Should be expanded, not eliminated
Was unconstitutional under the Bill of Rights
quiz.e: Jackson saw the Bank as favoring wealthy elites and vetoed its re-charter as part of the 'Bank War.'

quiz.q: The Nullification Crisis (1832-33) centered on South Carolina's claim that:
o: Slavery should be abolished immediately throughout the Southern states
The president had no veto power over acts passed by Congress
The Second Bank of the United States should be abolished by executive order
States could nullify federal laws (the tariff) they deemed unconstitutional
quiz.e: South Carolina argued it could nullify the federal tariff, testing the balance of federal versus state power.

quiz.q: William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator advocated for:
o: Gradual, compensated emancipation
Immediate abolition of slavery
Colonization of freed slaves to Africa
Expansion of slavery westward
quiz.e: Garrison was a leading voice for the immediate, uncompensated abolition of slavery.

quiz.q: Manifest Destiny is best defined as:
o: A treaty ending the Mexican-American War and setting the Rio Grande boundary
The belief that American expansion across the continent was inevitable and divinely sanctioned
A Supreme Court ruling on slavery that declared Congress could not restrict it in territories
An economic policy of protective tariffs to promote American manufacturing
quiz.e: Manifest Destiny was the widely held ideological justification for continental American expansion.

quiz.q: The Mexican Cession resulted from:
o: The Louisiana Purchase
The Mexican-American War (1846-48)
The War of 1812
The Missouri Compromise
quiz.e: The U.S. victory in the Mexican-American War brought California and the New Mexico territory into U.S. possession.

quiz.q: Which best characterizes the antebellum middle class ideal of womanhood, or 'cult of domesticity'?
o: Women's proper sphere was the home, as moral guardians of the family
Women should work exclusively in factories and earn wages equal to men's
Women should hold political office as reformers of public morality
Women were excluded from religious life and left moral teaching to men
quiz.e: As industrial work moved outside the home, a new ideology idealized women's role within domestic, moral spheres.

quiz.q: Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase (1803) created a constitutional dilemma because:
o: Jefferson was a strict constructionist but the purchase required a loose interpretation of federal power
It required Congressional approval that never came, leaving the purchase in legal limbo
It violated the Bill of Rights by taking land from Native peoples without consent
It was rejected by the Supreme Court as an unconstitutional exercise of presidential power
quiz.e: Jefferson, who favored strict construction, had to stretch his constitutional views to justify the purchase's constitutionality.

quiz.q: Horace Mann's education reforms primarily promoted:
o: Private religious schools funded by churches and open only to wealthy families
Common (public) schools accessible to all children
The abolition of universities in favor of vocational training programs
Military academies designed to train officers for the expanding army
quiz.e: Mann championed the common school movement, advocating for free, publicly funded education.

quiz.q: The Compromise of 1850 included all of the following EXCEPT:
o: California admitted as a free state
A stronger Fugitive Slave Act
Popular sovereignty in Utah and New Mexico territories
Immediate abolition of slavery nationwide
quiz.e: The Compromise did not abolish slavery; it balanced free/slave state admission and strengthened fugitive slave enforcement.

quiz.q: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) is significant because it:
o: Repealed the Missouri Compromise line by introducing popular sovereignty, leading to 'Bleeding Kansas'
Ended slavery in the territories by extending the Missouri Compromise line westward
Established the Republican Party's first presidential victory in the 1856 election
Resolved the sectional slavery debate peacefully by splitting the territories evenly
quiz.e: By allowing territories to vote on slavery, the Act effectively nullified the Missouri Compromise and caused violent conflict.

quiz.q: The Dred Scott v. Sandford decision (1857) ruled that:
o: Enslaved people were citizens with full rights, and Congress could ban slavery in territories
Slavery was unconstitutional, and fugitive slaves could not be returned to owners
States could nullify federal law, and Northern states could refuse fugitive slave laws
Enslaved people were not citizens, and Congress could not ban slavery in territories
quiz.e: The ruling denied Black citizenship and struck down congressional power to restrict slavery in territories, inflaming the North.

quiz.q: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) applied to:
o: All enslaved people in the United States, including border states
Enslaved people only in Confederate-held territory
Only enslaved people in Washington, D.C.
No one immediately, only a future promise
quiz.e: It freed enslaved people in Confederate territory only, not in the loyal border states, as a wartime measure.

quiz.q: Which battle is considered the war's turning point that also enabled the Emancipation Proclamation?
o: Fort Sumter
Antietam
Appomattox
Bull Run
quiz.e: The Union's tactical success (or at least non-defeat) at Antietam (1862) gave Lincoln the opening to issue the Proclamation.

quiz.q: The 14th Amendment (1868) is best known for establishing:
o: Birthright citizenship and equal protection under the law
The abolition of slavery throughout the United States
Voting rights for all men regardless of race or previous servitude
Direct election of senators by popular vote in each state
quiz.e: The 14th Amendment granted citizenship to all born in the U.S. and guaranteed equal protection of the laws.

quiz.q: The Freedmen's Bureau provided which service during Reconstruction?
o: Education, food, and legal aid to formerly enslaved people
Military weapons and supplies to former Confederates rebuilding their states
Enforcement of voting rights for Black Americans in the Northern states
Land grants given exclusively to Northern investors who moved South
